questions.q: Write the balanced half-reactions occurring at the anode and cathode of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell using concentrated NaOH electrolyte, and the overall cell reaction.
questions.a:
Anode (oxidation): 2H₂(g) + 4OH⁻(aq) → 4H₂O(l) + 4e⁻  
Cathode (reduction): O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻(aq)  
Overall: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)  
A wrong answer (e.g., using H⁺ instead of OH⁻, or unbalanced electrons) reveals the student does not recognize the alkaline medium or cannot balance redox half-reactions in basic solution — a prerequisite skill from Class 11 (c11_chem_cbse_08_003).

questions.q: Why are porous carbon electrodes impregnated with platinum or palladium used in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell instead of solid metal plates?
questions.a: Porous carbon provides high surface area for gas diffusion (H₂ and O₂) into the electrolyte, while Pt/Pd catalysts lower the activation energy for the electrode reactions (especially the slow oxygen reduction). Solid metal plates would not allow gas permeation and would have insufficient surface area. A wrong answer (e.g., "to conduct electricity better") shows confusion between electronic conduction (metal) and electrocatalysis at the triple-phase boundary (gas/electrolyte/electrode).

questions.q: Calculate the standard EMF of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell at 298 K given: E°(O₂/H₂O, OH⁻) = +0.40 V and E°(H₂O/H₂, OH⁻) = -0.83 V. Both are reduction potentials.
questions.a:
E°_cell = E°_cathode - E°_anode = E°(O₂ reduction) - E°(H₂ oxidation as reduction) = 0.40 V - (-0.83 V) = 1.23 V.  
Steps: (1) Identify cathode (O₂ reduction) and anode (H₂ oxidation). (2) Use given reduction potentials. (3) Apply E°_cell = E°_red,cathode - E°_red,anode. (4) Compute: 0.40 - (-0.83) = 1.23 V.  
A wrong answer (e.g., 0.40 - 0.83 = -0.43 V) reveals sign convention error: using oxidation potential for anode instead of reduction potential, or subtracting incorrectly. This is a classic JEE/NEET trap from c12_chem_cbse_02_002.

questions.q: A fuel cell operates at 70% efficiency while a thermal power plant operates at 40%. If both use the same amount of hydrogen fuel (ΔH_comb = -286 kJ/mol), how much more electrical energy (in kJ) does the fuel cell produce per mole of H₂?
questions.a:
Fuel cell electrical energy = 0.70 × 286 = 200.2 kJ/mol H₂  
Thermal plant electrical energy = 0.40 × 286 = 114.4 kJ/mol H₂  
Difference = 200.2 - 114.4 = 85.8 kJ/mol H₂  
A wrong answer (e.g., using 100% efficiency or confusing ΔH with ΔG) shows inability to apply efficiency concept to energy conversion — a cross-link with thermodynamics (c11_chem_cbse_06_007) and physics (energy conversion efficiency).

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is a primary battery because it cannot be recharged." Is it correct? Justify.
questions.a: Incorrect. A fuel cell is NOT a battery (primary or secondary). In a battery, reactants are stored internally and deplete over time. In a fuel cell, reactants (H₂, O₂) are supplied continuously from external reservoirs — it is an open system. It does not "recharge" because it never "discharges" in the battery sense; it simply stops when fuel supply stops. A student calling it a primary battery confuses energy storage (battery) with energy conversion (fuel cell) — a fundamental distinction from c12_chem_cbse_02_008.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to demonstrate the working principle of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell using school laboratory materials. List materials, procedure, and expected observation.
questions.a:
Materials: Two Pt electrodes, 1 M NaOH, H₂ gas (from Zn + HCl), O₂ gas (from H₂O₂ + MnO₂), voltmeter, beaker, gas delivery tubes.  
Procedure: (1) Fill beaker with 1 M NaOH. (2) Immerse Pt electrodes. (3) Bubble H₂ at one electrode (anode), O₂ at other (cathode). (4) Connect voltmeter.  
Observation: Voltage ~0.9-1.0 V (less than 1.23 V due to overpotential).  
A poor answer (e.g., using graphite rods without catalyst, or expecting 1.23 V exactly) reveals lack of understanding of overpotential, catalyst necessity, and real-world non-ideality — key for JEE Advanced experimental questions.
